text: Sharing individual reports the way Lesson 72 covered works perfectly well for one or two people at a time. Once an entire department or a whole organization needs access to a full collection of dashboards and reports together, you package all of it into an app instead.

Apps show up in their very own dedicated list, entirely distinct from the workspace they originally came from. Users viewing an app can filter, sort, and drill into every visual freely, but they can never actually modify anything sitting underneath what you originally published.

Every single app starts from one place: Create app, sitting right there in the workspace list view, exactly one level up from the workspace itself. From there you move through three tabs in sequence — Setup, Content, and Audience.
Setup captures the app's name, its description, and a theme color — genuinely the very first thing app users see before they've even opened the app itself, so it's worth getting right.

Audiences are really the true power behind the whole feature. Create a Sales team audience and a Product team audience, and each one can see entirely different content, hidden or shown individually, from the exact same underlying app — with its own separate reshare and build permissions too.

One published app, genuinely many possible views depending entirely on who's looking at it. Remember that a direct link still bypasses audience hiding, so hiding content is for navigation clarity, never for real security. Lesson 74 covers the very last piece of this chapter: dashboards themselves, back in the Power BI service.
